notes.trap: Without `fmt`, `to_date(...)` uses CAST rules, so only ISO-like strings such as 'yyyy-MM-dd[ ...]' parse. Other layouts silently return NULL because ANSI is off by default. Pattern letters are case-sensitive: 'MM' is month and 'mm' is minute.
Without a format, an offset in the string is honoured. The instant is converted and displayed in the session time zone, so the wall-clock value changes.
When no format is given, a zone or offset in the input is silently dropped rather than applied. The local date-time is kept as written, unlike `to_timestamp(...)`, which converts it.
The default format is 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss', not CAST rules. A date-only string without an explicit format fails to parse and returns NULL when ANSI is off.
The string is interpreted in the session time zone. The documented example value 1460041200 assumes America/Los_Angeles; under UTC the same call returns a different number.

It shifts the wall-clock value by treating the input as local time in the given zone and returning the UTC wall clock. It is the inverse of `from_utc_timestamp(...)`, and the two are easy to swap by mistake.

The argument order is (date, fmt), the reverse of `date_trunc(...)`. Only year, quarter, month and week units are supported. 'DD'/'DAY' or swapped arguments silently return NULL instead of raising an error.
With ANSI off (the default) it behaves the same as `to_timestamp(...)`: unparseable input gives NULL. It only differs when ANSI mode is on, where `to_timestamp(...)` would raise an error.
Dates before 1970-01-01 give negative day counts rather than NULL or an error.
The documentation says it truncates sub-second precision, but it actually floors. For timestamps before the epoch, a fractional second rounds toward negative infinity, not toward zero.
Sub-millisecond precision is floored, not truncated toward zero. Pre-epoch timestamps therefore drop to the next lower millisecond.
It is 0-based starting Monday (Sunday = 6). `dayofweek(...)` is 1-based starting Sunday (Sunday = 1).
It uses ISO-8601 weeks, so early-January dates can fall in week 52 or 53 of the previous year.
Windows are aligned to 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC, not to the data. Because the epoch was a Thursday, '1 week' windows start on Thursdays unless you pass a start_time offset.
notes.example_sql: SELECT window.start FROM VALUES (TIMESTAMP'2021-01-04 12:00:00') AS t(b) GROUP BY window(b, '1 week')

notes.trap: It returns window.end minus one microsecond, not window.end. This reflects the exclusive upper bound of the window.
notes.example_sql: SELECT window_time(window) FROM (SELECT window FROM VALUES (TIMESTAMP'2021-01-01 00:01:00') AS t(b) GROUP BY window(b, '5 minutes'))

notes.trap: String arguments are implicitly cast to DATE. An invalid calendar date silently becomes NULL with ANSI off instead of raising an error.
